19 PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY AND GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT (J24, J25) 740 × 560
LAB SUMMARY AND ABSTRACT FIGURE required by the journal · useful regardless
PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY · 148 WORDS
Cells grown in the laboratory are used to test new gene-editing tools. We found that these cells stop responding to one common editing method after they have been grown and split about eighteen times — the success rate falls from roughly four in ten to fewer than one in twenty, and it does not recover. We tested whether poor-quality chemicals were to blame and they were not. Laboratories that keep using older cells may be repeating experiments that cannot work, without knowing why. Our practical recommendation is to freeze a large stock of young cells at the start of a project and return to it, rather than continuing to grow the same batch.

RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS · J2911 OF 11 ADDRESSED
REVIEWER 2, POINT 4
YOUR RESPONSE
"The authors claim the effect is not due to reagent quality but test only two lots from a single supplier. This is insufficient."
We agree. We have added a third lot from an independent supplier (new Fig. S3) and narrowed the claim in the abstract from "reagent quality" to "reagent lot".
changed §2.3, abstract, Fig. S3 · see the diff
"Figure 2 does not distinguish the two lots."
Corrected — the lots are now coloured separately and n is stated per point.
figure rebuilt from DS-1174 v2.1
"The mechanism should be demonstrated, not inferred."
Respectfully, we disagree that this is required here. We have removed the mechanistic claim entirely rather than assert it — the paper now reports the threshold and its practical consequence, and cites Nakamura et al. for the proposed mechanism.
disagreement, stated plainly · reviewers respect this more than a hedge
EVERY RESPONSE LINKS TO A CHANGE
"We have added a third lot" points at the actual diff, the new figure and the dataset version. A response letter that claims changes the manuscript does not contain is the fastest route to a second round.
EXPORT
Produces the two files every journal wants: a point-by-point response letter and a tracked-changes manuscript — generated from the same source, so they cannot disagree.
